Loans you already owe and your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months can lower that amount. The calculator subtracts what you owe. It returns the largest new loan allowed and the payment for the amount you want to borrow. Start with Vested account balance, then enter any Plan loans you owe now and your Highest plan-loan balance, last 12 months. Add the Loan amount you want, Interest rate (annual percentage rate, APR), Term (years), Payments per year and Loan purpose to see the repayment figures and any rule warnings. In our internal modeling, we applied the loan-limit formula to a $60,000 vested balance with no earlier loans. The limit on all plan loans together was $30,000, leaving $30,000 available for a new loan. For a $10,000 loan at an example 8% APR, the payment was $202.76 per month over 5 years. Total interest was $2,165.84, and total repaid was $12,165.84. Those payment figures use a level-payment schedule. They do not establish the rate your plan would charge. Change the inputs below to see how a different loan amount, rate or payment schedule changes the result. $30,000 largest new loan at $60,000 vested $202.76 payment on $10,000 over 5 years $2,166 total interest Share Interactive — edit any field How the Loan Limit Is Calculated Under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(A) , the limit on all plan loans together is the smaller of two amounts. The first starts at $50,000 and falls by the amount your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded what you owe today. The second is the greater of half your vested balance or $10,000. The calculator compares those two amounts, then subtracts Plan loans you owe now to show room for a new loan. If you have borrowed before, the limit on all loans is not the amount you can take out today. Enter the highest balance even if you have since paid down that loan, because the earlier balance can reduce the $50,000 prong. Vested balance Owed now 12-month peak Limit on all loans Room for a new loan $15,000 None None $10,000 $10,000 $60,000 None None $30,000 $30,000 $100,000 None None $50,000 $50,000 $200,000 None None $50,000 $50,000 $200,000 $10,000 $20,000 $40,000 $30,000 $200,000 $20,000 $50,000 $20,000 $0 The $15,000 balance produces a $10,000 limit because half the vested balance is $7,500 and the statutory floor is higher. A plan may also cap a loan at your vested balance. At a $100,000 vested balance with nothing owed, half the balance reaches the $50,000 cap. A higher vested balance does not raise that cap: the $200,000 example with no loans also has a $50,000 limit. The prior-loan example shows why the two subtractions must stay separate. With $10,000 owed and a $20,000 peak, the peak exceeds today's balance by $10,000, reducing the $50,000 prong to $40,000. The calculator then subtracts the $10,000 still owed from the $40,000 limit, leaving $30,000 for a new loan. Subtracting the $10,000 a second time would count it twice and wrongly leave $20,000 of room. In the last table row, the peak reduces that prong to $20,000, which equals the amount already owed. The result is no room for another loan under the federal cap, even though the vested balance is higher. Repayment Rules the Calculator Checks A general-purpose plan loan must be repayable within 5 years under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(B) and (C) . The statute makes an exception for a loan used to buy a dwelling that will become the participant's main home within a reasonable time. It also requires substantially level payments at least quarterly. Choose General purpose or Buy a main home under Loan purpose so the calculator can check the term you entered. It warns when a general-purpose term exceeds 5 years or when Payments per year is less often than quarterly. A green note means the entered amount, term and payment frequency fit the federal rules the calculator checks. It does not mean your plan offers loans. The calculator also warns when Loan amount you want exceeds Largest new loan allowed. Under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(1) , the portion outside the qualifying loan rules is treated as a distribution. Use the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator for a tax estimate rather than treating that excess as an ordinary loan payment. For payments, the calculator divides APR by Payments per year to get the periodic rate. It multiplies Term (years) by Payments per year to get the number of payments, then applies payment = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n). Each payment covers that period's interest. The remainder reduces the loan balance. Payment frequency changes the schedule too: at an example 8%, the same $10,000 loan over 5 years has 20 quarterly payments of $611.57 each. At that rate, paying every two weeks produces 130 payments of $93.45 each. A longer permitted main-home term can lower each payment while increasing total interest in the supplied example. A $30,000 loan at an example 8% costs $608.29 per month over 5 years, with $6,497.51 in total interest. Over 15 years, the main-home example costs $286.70 per month, with $21,605.21 in total interest. Run your own amount and rate before relying on any example payment. The federal limit and repayment rules determine whether the amount qualifies as a loan rather than a distribution, while the plan document decides whether borrowing is available at all. If the plan document has no loan provision, this calculator cannot make a loan available. Borrowing from a Solo 401(k) The same federal loan-limit formula applies to an owner-only 401(k), so a solo 401k loan calculator needs no separate limit setting. The plan document must provide for loans, and a provision alone does not establish that a participant loan avoids a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. 4975(d)(1) . An owner is generally a key employee under 26 U.S.C. 416(i) , so interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible for any period the owner is a key employee ( 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(3) ). Read the solo section of the 401(k) loan rules guide , then enter your vested balance in the calculator above. What the Calculator Does Not Include The calculator does not include plan fees or determine your plan's interest rate or loan limits. Enter the interest rate and loan amount you want in the calculator. The calculator does not estimate income tax or additional tax if a loan is treated as a distribution. Use the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator for a tax estimate, and ask a tax professional about a missed payment. The calculator assigns no market return to money while it is out of the plan and does not determine where repayments are credited. Account for the borrowed money's time out of the market separately. Whether interest you repay is credited to your account depends on the plan document. The calculator does not compare a plan loan with another borrowing source. Use the 401(k) loan vs home equity line of credit (HELOC) comparison to weigh the borrowing choices. Frequently asked questions How are 401k loan amounts calculated? The federal limit on all your plan loans is the smaller of a reduced $50,000 cap or the greater of half your vested balance and $10,000. The cap falls by any amount your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded what you owe today. Subtract loans you owe now from the resulting limit to find room for a new loan. With $60,000 vested and no earlier loans, the limit and room for a new loan are both $30,000. How much would a $10,000 401(k) loan cost per month over 5 years? A $10,000 loan paid monthly over 5 years costs $202.76 per month at an example 8% APR. At example rates of 6% and 10%, the payments are $193.33 and $212.47 per month, respectively. These are example rates. A plan sets its own rate. Enter the interest rate from your plan terms in this calculator to see your own payment. How many 401(k) loans can you have at once? The federal loan-limit text states no maximum number of simultaneous plan loans. It counts every outstanding plan loan toward the limit. Your plan document decides whether loans are available and whether it limits their number. Enter all Plan loans you owe now to calculate the room left for another loan. Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)? A solo 401(k) can provide for participant loans, but its plan document must allow them. The same federal loan-limit formula applies to an owner-only plan, and a plan provision alone does not settle the prohibited-transaction requirements. Read the solo section of the 401(k) loan rules guide before using the calculator for a proposed loan. What happens if I do not repay a 401(k) loan? A plan loan that fails to meet the qualifying loan rules can be treated as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(1). The calculator does not determine the tax consequences of a missed payment. Ask a tax professional to confirm those consequences, and use the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator for a tax estimate. The hard money loan calculator shows that cost alongside your loan amount, cash to close, monthly interest-only payment, and balloon payoff. It also returns loan-to-cost and loan-to-after-repair-value percentages. Enter an after-repair value (ARV) to see profit before tax. Start with the purchase price, rehab budget, and terms from your lender quote. A hard money loan here means a short-term loan with points and fees at closing, interest-only payments, and repayment of the full balance at exit. The starting points, rate and months are example inputs with no lender data behind them. Swap in the points and hold time from your lender quote. In our internal modeling, we ran one example deal and found a $20,900 total financing cost on a $230,000 loan held for 6 months. The example uses a $200,000 purchase and a $50,000 rehab budget. The lender advances 90% of the purchase and 100% of the rehab, with a 12% annual percentage rate (APR). Closing charges are 2 points and $2,500 in other fees. The result includes $13,800 in interest and $7,100 in points and fees. Repayment of the $230,000 loan balance is a separate balloon payoff, so it does not appear as another financing charge. You can reproduce the example with the starting inputs, then enter your own terms to see how the cost changes. $20,900 total financing cost on the example terms $2,300 monthly interest-only payment 92% loan to cost Share Interactive — edit any field How the Cost Adds Up Total financing cost adds the points paid at closing, lender and other fees, interest during the months held, and any extension fee. Points equal the loan amount multiplied by the points percentage. For each month, interest equals the outstanding balance multiplied by the APR and divided by 12. Piece Example amount Loan $230,000 Points $4,600 Other fees $2,500 Interest-only payment $2,300 a month Interest over 6 months $13,800 Total financing cost $20,900 Balloon payoff $230,000 Cash to close $27,100 The loan combines $180,000 advanced against the purchase with $50,000 advanced for rehab. The $20,000 down payment, $4,600 in points, and $2,500 in other fees make cash to close $27,100. Interest-only payments cover interest while the balance remains outstanding. In this example, the $2,300 monthly payment does not pay down the $230,000 loan. Simple annualized cost divides total financing cost by the loan amount and then by the years held. It is 18.17% for this example, which includes points and fees as well as interest. It is not an internal rate of return (IRR): the calculation does not use the dates of individual cash flows to produce an IRR. Loan to Cost and Loan to ARV Explained Loan to cost (LTC) divides the loan amount by the purchase price plus the rehab budget. For the example, the $230,000 loan divided by the $200,000 purchase and $50,000 rehab budget gives 92%. This percentage describes the share of those project costs covered by the modeled loan. It does not include financing charges or other holding costs in the denominator. Loan to after-repair value (ARV) divides the loan amount by the after-repair value you enter. At an example ARV of $330,000, the $230,000 loan produces a loan-to-ARV figure of 69.7%. Leave ARV blank if you only need the loan-cost calculation. The loan-to-ARV and profit figures need an ARV input. The profit calculation starts with ARV and subtracts selling costs, purchase price, rehab budget, total financing cost, and other holding costs. The starting inputs leave ARV, selling costs and holding costs blank, so enter $330,000, 6% and $1,000 a month to reproduce this profit. At $330,000 ARV and 6% selling costs, the modeled selling costs are $19,800. Other holding costs of $1,000 a month add up to $6,000 over 6 months. With those inputs, Profit before tax is $33,300. That figure counts the $20,900 financing cost as an expense, alongside the purchase and rehab costs. The balloon payoff is not subtracted again: the purchase and rehab amounts already represent the project spending financed in part by the loan. What Moves the Total Most Holding time changes the example's financing cost by $2,300 for each additional month at the full loan balance. The calculator's What moves the total table also changes points and APR while keeping the other example inputs fixed. These figures show how much each specified change moves the $20,900 starting total. Change Total financing cost Change from example Hold for 3 months $14,000 $6,900 lower Hold for 9 months $27,800 $6,900 higher Charge 1 point $18,600 $2,300 lower Charge 3 points $23,200 $2,300 higher Use 10% APR $18,600 $2,300 lower Use 14% APR $23,200 $2,300 higher A point equals 1% of the loan amount. On the $230,000 example loan, changing the charge by one point changes closing cost by $2,300. The interest-rate rows show the same dollar change for the stated APR changes over the example holding period. They do not tell you what a lender will quote. An extension can change both interest and fees. On the example loan, a 3-month extension with a 1% extension fee adds $6,900 of interest and a $2,300 fee. That is $9,200 more in financing cost, bringing the total to $30,100. The extension months accrue interest on the full loan balance. The rehab funding choice changes when interest begins on the rehab advance. If rehab money is Funded at closing, the full loan accrues interest from the first month. If it is Drawn evenly each month, the modeled rehab balance grows in equal monthly portions. The purchase advance remains outstanding throughout. For the example's 6-month hold, even draws reduce interest from $13,800 to $12,550. Total financing cost falls from $20,900 to $19,650. Select the funding method that matches the schedule you are modeling rather than treating the two totals as interchangeable quotes. On the example loan, each extra month held, each extra point and each 2 points of APR add the same $2,300. Months held can swing further because a late payoff can stack several months. The hard money loan calculator cannot supply a lender quote. If you need a quoted rate or fee, obtain those terms from a lender before using its output to compare financing costs. Type your quoted points and months held into the calculator above, then read the Total financing cost line. What the Calculator Does Not Include The calculator does not subtract income tax from profit. For the tax issue associated with a short-term flip, read flipping houses and its tax trap and keep the displayed profit labeled before tax. Draw inspection fees are not included automatically. If your terms list them, add their amount to Lender, document and other fees. Default interest and prepayment minimums are not modeled. Read the repayment terms in the quote before relying on the displayed interest total for a different payoff schedule. Profit before tax ignores any costs you have not entered, as well as tax. Enter the available selling and holding costs, and treat the result as a calculation based only on those inputs. The calculator does not compare this loan with a different short-term financing route. Use the bridge loan vs home equity line of credit (HELOC) comparison to examine that choice, then enter separate terms in the bridge loan calculator . Frequently asked questions How do you calculate loan to cost? Divide the loan amount by the purchase price plus the rehab budget. The example combines a $200,000 purchase and a $50,000 rehab budget. A $230,000 loan against those costs gives a 92% loan-to-cost figure. This calculation uses the stated purchase and rehab costs and does not add interest or fees to that denominator. Are hard money loans interest only? This calculator models interest-only payments each month and repayment of the full balance at exit. Its monthly payment does not reduce the balloon payoff. Your lender's terms determine whether the loan you are considering follows that structure. Use the payment and payoff terms in your quote when interpreting the results. How much do points add to a hard money loan? Points add the loan amount multiplied by the points percentage to closing cost. On the $230,000 example loan, 2 points add $4,600. Each point changes that loan's closing cost by $2,300. Points are included in Total financing cost even though they are paid at closing rather than through monthly interest. What does an extension cost? An extension adds interest for the extra months and any extension fee entered. In the example, 3 extra months add $6,900 in interest. A 1% fee adds another $2,300, bringing the extension's added financing cost to $9,200. The calculator applies interest during extension months to the full loan balance. This bridge loan calculator returns that total cost and the monthly outlay for carrying both homes. It also returns the net proceeds left after the sale pays off the old mortgage, the bridge loan and selling costs. Start with the expected sale price and old mortgage payoff. Then enter the bridge loan terms and the number of months you expect to carry both homes. The sale price, loan and months already in the calculator are made-up example inputs. Replace them with your own sale details and quote. In our internal modeling, we ran one example sale through the calculator and found a $7,000 bridge loan cost after 6 months. The example uses a $400,000 sale price, a $200,000 old mortgage payoff, and a $100,000 bridge loan. At 10% annual percentage rate (APR) with 2% origination, the loan accrues $5,000 in interest and $2,000 in fees. Selling costs of 6% leave $69,000 in net proceeds. Enter your own terms below to see how a different sale date changes the result. $7,000 bridge cost over 6 months on the example terms $69,000 net proceeds from the old home Share Interactive — edit any field What a Bridge Loan Costs Month by Month Bridge interest is simple interest: multiply the loan by its APR, divide by 12, then multiply by the months until the old home sells. Fees equal the loan multiplied by the origination percentage, plus other fees charged once. Bridge loan cost adds those fees to interest. The calculation assumes interest is repaid from the sale proceeds at payoff. The example below holds the sale price, loan terms, selling costs, and monthly home payments fixed. Only the time until sale changes. Each row shows the bridge cost alongside the separate outlay for carrying both homes. Months to sell Interest Bridge cost Overlap outlay Net proceeds 3 $2,500 $4,500 $12,900 $71,500 6 $5,000 $7,000 $25,800 $69,000 9 $7,500 $9,500 $38,700 $66,500 12 $10,000 $12,000 $51,600 $64,000 Monthly overlap outlay adds the new mortgage payment to the old home's monthly carrying costs. Enter the old mortgage payment, taxes, insurance, and utilities in that carrying-cost field. With a $2,500 new mortgage payment and $1,800 in old home carrying costs, the outlay is $4,300 each month. The overlap total tells you how much cash you need for those home payments while waiting for a sale. It is separate from the bridge loan cost shown in the table. Under the calculator's payoff assumption, bridge interest reduces sale proceeds rather than appearing in the monthly overlap outlay. Selling costs equal the sale price multiplied by the selling-cost percentage. Net proceeds then subtract the old mortgage payoff, bridge loan, bridge cost, and selling costs from the sale price. In the example, $24,000 of selling costs leaves $69,000 after those deductions. The origination fee is charged once in this calculation, even if the sale takes longer than expected. If the old home sells after 0 months, the example bridge cost is the $2,000 fee alone. With no origination fee, the 6-month bridge cost falls to $5,000 and net proceeds rise to $71,000. Enter any other one-time fees separately so they appear in the bridge cost. How Much You Can Borrow The calculator estimates a borrowing ceiling only when you enter your lender's maximum combined loan-to-value limit. It multiplies the expected sale price by that limit and subtracts the old mortgage payoff. That gives you a figure to compare with your planned bridge loan. For the example sale, an entered limit of 80% produces a maximum of $120,000. The calculation applies 80% to the $400,000 expected sale price, then subtracts the $200,000 old mortgage payoff. The entered limit is an example. It is no standard lender limit and no loan offer. Your lender's quote supplies the limit, rate, fees, and term. If you do not have a combined loan-to-value figure, leave that optional field empty rather than treating the example as an available borrowing amount. You can still estimate bridge cost and net proceeds using the loan amount and terms you enter. A higher bridge loan amount affects more than the amount repaid at sale. Because interest is calculated from the loan amount, changing the bridge amount also changes interest and the net proceeds calculation. Origination fees change with the loan amount when you enter an origination percentage. Use the amount you intend to borrow when comparing the calculator's cost with the cash you expect from the old home. When the Old Home Sells Late A later sale raises bridge interest and extends the monthly outlay for carrying both homes. In the example, each extra month adds $833.33 of bridge interest and lowers net proceeds by $833.33. The home payments continue separately at $4,300 a month under the example inputs. Use the calculator's "If the old home sells in" table to compare sale dates. It shows the entered timeline alongside 3, 6, and 9 months, so you can see the cost of a delay without changing the inputs repeatedly. The Copy results button lets you keep the figures from the scenario you entered. The optional Alternative cost, per month field compares the bridge's fees and interest with a monthly cost you enter. Break-even months equal bridge fees divided by the alternative's monthly cost minus bridge monthly interest. The calculation produces a break-even point only when the alternative costs more per month than bridge interest. Against an example alternative costing $1,500 a month with no up-front fee, the bridge costs less once the old home takes more than 3.0 months to sell. If the home sells sooner, the bridge costs more than that alternative. If the alternative costs no more than the bridge's $833.33 monthly interest, the bridge never costs less under this comparison. A sale may also leave too little to repay everything. If the old mortgage payoff rises from $200,000 to $300,000, the example produces negative $31,000 in net proceeds. The calculator warns when the sale does not cover the old mortgage, bridge loan, bridge cost, and selling costs. That result means you would bring cash to closing. For another way to pay for the overlap, compare a bridge loan with a home equity line of credit (HELOC) in our bridge loan vs HELOC guide. For a related guide, see the guide to buying and selling a house at the same time . Bridge cost rises with the months until sale, so price a timeline that fits your plan before committing. Enter your own months to sell and lender quote in the bridge loan calculator above, then read the Bridge loan cost line. The calculator leaves out taxes on the sale. Keep any sale-related tax amount separate from the net proceeds shown here. The calculator does not model prepayment terms or lender-specific rules. Use the terms in your lender quote when deciding how the calculated cost applies to a loan offer. The calculator does not price an investment purchase financed with a different short-term loan. A loan from a qualified employer plan is treated as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A) unless it stays within the amount limit, is repaid within 5 years (longer if it buys your main home), and is repaid in substantially level payments at least quarterly. To see how a permanent withdrawal works, read How to Withdraw From a 401(k) or try the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator . Tools for this journey 401(k) loan calculator → 401(k) early withdrawal calculator → How a 401(k) Loan Works and How Much You Can Borrow Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(A) , a new loan plus all your other outstanding loans from the plan must not exceed the lesser of two limits. The first limit is $50,000, reduced by the excess (if any) of your highest outstanding loan balance during the one-year period ending the day before the new loan is made over your outstanding balance on the day it is made. The second limit is the greater of one-half of your vested balance (your nonforfeitable accrued benefit under the plan) or $10,000. These three illustrations of the formula assume no prior loans. They are examples, not advice. A participant with a $15,000 vested balance: one-half of the balance is $7,500. Because the formula uses the greater of one-half of the vested balance or $10,000, the second limit is $10,000. Comparing $10,000 to the $50,000 maximum, the lesser figure is $10,000. The borrowing cap is $10,000. A participant with a $60,000 vested balance: one-half of the vested balance is $30,000. That figure is greater than $10,000. Comparing $30,000 to the $50,000 ceiling, the lesser figure is $30,000. The borrowing cap is $30,000. A participant with a $200,000 vested balance: one-half of the vested balance is $100,000. That figure exceeds $10,000, but federal law caps the maximum borrowing amount at the lesser of that figure or $50,000. The borrowing cap is $50,000. To run your own numbers, use the 401(k) loan calculator . Can a Solo 401(k) Lend to Its Owner? Yes, a solo 401(k) can lend to its owner when the plan document provides for loans, and the same 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2) limits apply. Lending between a plan and a disqualified person is generally a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(c)(1)(B) . The statute provides an exception for a loan to a disqualified person who is a plan participant or beneficiary, but a provision allowing loans is only one part of that exception. Under § 4975(d)(1), the loan must meet all five conditions: The loan must be available to all such participants or beneficiaries on a reasonably equivalent basis. Highly compensated employees must not be able to borrow larger amounts than other employees can borrow. The loan must follow specific provisions for loans set out in the plan. The loan must bear a reasonable rate of interest. The loan must be adequately secured. The loan exception is unavailable for lending to an owner of an individual retirement plan under § 4975(f)(6). A Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) IRA, a Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) IRA, or a traditional individual retirement account (IRA) therefore cannot lend to its owner. That restriction does not categorically bar a solo 401(k) loan. For a different borrowing source, read 401(k) loan vs HELOC . An owner is generally a key employee because 26 U.S.C. § 416(i)(1)(A) includes a 5-percent owner in that category. Under § 72(p)(3), interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible during a period when the owner is a key employee. The plan document and its administrator determine whether a given loan meets the loan conditions. Run your balance through the 401(k) loan calculator . Repayment Rules and the Principal Residence Exception Federal law requires a 401(k) loan to be repaid within 5 years under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(i) . The terms of the loan agreement must require full repayment within that 5-year window from the date the loan is made. A loan term longer than 5 years fails the repayment rule unless the home purchase exception applies. The 5-year limit does not apply to a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence ( 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(ii) ). That is determined when the loan is made. The longer term for such a loan is set by your plan, so ask your plan administrator. In addition to the term limit, 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(C) requires substantially level amortization of the loan over its entire term. Payments must be made not less frequently than quarterly. What Happens If a 401(k) Loan Is Not Repaid A plan loan is treated as having been received as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A) if it does not meet the amount, 5-year term, and quarterly level-payment rules. A distribution can bring federal income tax. In addition to regular income tax, an early distribution can trigger an extra tax penalty. According to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Topic 558 , the law imposes a 10% additional tax on certain early distributions from retirement plans. Early distributions are generally distributions received before age 59½, though exceptions exist as detailed by the IRS. If a 401(k) loan balance is treated as a distribution to a borrower who has not reached age 59½, that borrower can face both income tax and the 10% additional tax on the unpaid amount. A separate rollover rule applies to a qualified plan loan offset amount. Under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A) , the ordinary rollover window to deposit distributed funds into an eligible retirement plan or Individual Retirement Account (IRA) is 60 days after the distribution is received. However, for a qualified plan loan offset amount, 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C)(i) provides an extended rollover deadline. You can complete a rollover of a qualified plan loan offset amount up to the due date, including tax extensions, for filing your federal income tax return for the tax year in which the amount is treated as distributed from the plan. Whether an offset qualifies requires specific analysis, so ask your plan administrator or a professional tax advisor about your situation. Plan-Specific Rules and Interest Deductibility Restrictions Federal statute authorizes employer plans to offer loans, but it does not require any plan to do so. Whether an employer retirement plan permits borrowing at all is decided entirely by the employer's plan document. If your plan does permit loans, the plan document also determines the application fees, ongoing administrative charges, the specific interest rate charged, the maximum number of loans you may have outstanding at one time, and the exact default procedures. Interest on a plan loan is not deductible in some cases, such as any period when you are a key employee or when the loan is secured by certain elective deferrals ( 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(3)(A) ). Ask your plan administrator or a tax professional whether either applies to you. Comparing a 401(k) Loan to Alternative Financing Options For another way to borrow, see our comparison of a 401(k) Loan vs HELOC . To explore debt payoff strategies, see our guide on How to Pay Off Debt . Next Steps for Requesting Your Plan Loan Documents Contact your employer's plan administrator to request a complete copy of the plan loan policy in writing. Review the document to confirm whether loans are permitted, the exact fees charged to originate and service the loan, the interest rate calculation method, and the plan's specific default timelines. Read your vested balance from your latest participant statement, then apply the lesser-of and greater-of formula from the first section. Frequently asked questions How much can I borrow from my 401(k)? Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(A), your loan plus all other outstanding plan loans must not exceed the lesser of $50,000 (reduced by any excess of your highest loan balance in the past year over your balance on the day the loan is made) or the greater of $10,000 or half your vested balance. With no prior loans, a $15,000 vested balance gives a $10,000 cap, $60,000 gives $30,000, and $200,000 gives $50,000. How long do I have to repay a 401(k) loan? Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(i), you must repay a 401(k) loan within 5 years from the date the loan is made. Repayment must occur through substantially level payments made at least quarterly over the term of the loan under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(C). The 5-year limit does not apply when loan proceeds are used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence. Do I pay taxes on a 401(k) loan? Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A), a loan from a qualified plan is treated as a distribution unless it meets the amount limit, the 5-year term, and the level quarterly payment rules. A distribution can bring regular income tax. If you are under age 59½, it can also bring the 10% additional tax described in IRS Topic 558, though exceptions exist. What happens to a 401(k) loan if I leave my job? What happens when you leave depends on your plan's default rules, so ask your plan administrator. If an unpaid balance is treated as a distribution, the ordinary rollover window is 60 days after the distribution is received (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A)). For a qualified plan loan offset amount, a rollover can be made up to the due date, including extensions, for filing the tax return for the year the amount is treated as distributed (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C)(i)). Ask your plan administrator or a tax professional whether your offset qualifies. Can I borrow from my 401(k) to buy a house? Yes, if your employer plan allows it. Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(ii), the 5-year repayment limit does not apply to a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence. The amount limit still applies, and repayment must still be made in substantially level payments at least quarterly. Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)? Yes, you can take a loan from a solo 401(k) if its plan document provides for loans, and the same limits under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) apply. Avoiding a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1) takes more than a plan provision. The loan must also meet the other conditions in that section, and the plan document and its administrator decide whether a given loan does. An IRA-based plan cannot lend to its owner under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(f)(6). For the full list of conditions, see the section "Can a Solo 401(k) Lend to Its Owner?" above. How does a solo 401(k) loan work? The loan must follow the same amount, term, and payment rules under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) and meet the other conditions in 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1). An owner is generally a key employee under 26 U.S.C. § 416(i)(1)(A)(ii). Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(3), interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible for any period the owner is a key employee. acceptedAnswer.text: What happens when you leave depends on your plan's default rules, so ask your plan administrator. If an unpaid balance is treated as a distribution, the ordinary rollover window is 60 days after the distribution is received (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A)). For a qualified plan loan offset amount, a rollover can be made up to the due date, including extensions, for filing the tax return for the year the amount is treated as distributed (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C)(i)). Ask your plan administrator or a tax professional whether your offset qualifies.

mainEntity.name: Can I borrow from my 401(k) to buy a house?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your employer plan allows it. Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(ii), the 5-year repayment limit does not apply to a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence. The amount limit still applies, and repayment must still be made in substantially level payments at least quarterly.

mainEntity.name: Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, you can take a loan from a solo 401(k) if its plan document provides for loans, and the same limits under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) apply. Avoiding a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1) takes more than a plan provision. The loan must also meet the other conditions in that section, and the plan document and its administrator decide whether a given loan does. An IRA-based plan cannot lend to its owner under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(f)(6). For the full list of conditions, see the section "Can a Solo 401(k) Lend to Its Owner?" above.

mainEntity.name: How does a solo 401(k) loan work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The loan must follow the same amount, term, and payment rules under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) and meet the other conditions in 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1). An owner is generally a key employee under 26 U.S.C. § 416(i)(1)(A)(ii). Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(3), interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible for any period the owner is a key employee. Use the 401(k) loan calculator to see the limit and payment for your balance.

By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated September 28, 2026 A 401(k) loan lets you borrow from your own retirement balance without a credit check or home lien, while a home equity line of credit (HELOC) lets you borrow against your home value without pulling money out of tax-advantaged investments. At ModernWallet, we evaluate consumer borrowing through total net worth impact, comparing a 401k loan vs HELOC by measuring default penalties, repayment timelines, and asset exposure. Choosing the wrong borrowing vehicle can either put your residence at risk of foreclosure or generate unexpected income taxes if your employment ends unexpectedly. Every borrower must weigh whether they prefer risking their future retirement security or pledging their physical home as collateral to secure liquidity today. 401(k) Loan vs HELOC: Side-by-Side 401(k) Loan HELOC Qualification requirements Requires no credit check, income verification, or property appraisal; availability depends on whether your employer plan permits participant loans Requires a formal credit check, proof of steady income, and a home appraisal to evaluate available home equity Maximum borrowing limit Capped under federal rules at the lesser of 50% of your vested account balance or $50,000 Determined by your lender based on your home value, existing mortgage balance, and maximum allowable loan-to-value ratio Destination of interest payments All interest payments go directly back into your own 401(k) account at a plan-determined interest rate All interest payments go directly to the commercial lending institution as compensation for the loan Default and job-loss consequences Unpaid balances after leaving an employer become taxable distributions subject to income taxes and potential early-withdrawal penalties Failure to meet monthly repayment obligations can result in default, severe credit damage, and eventual property foreclosure Tax deductibility of interest Interest is never tax-deductible because the borrower is paying interest back to their own personal retirement account Interest may be federally tax-deductible if proceeds are used to buy, build, or substantially improve the securing property Impact on investment growth Borrowed capital stops earning investment returns and market dividends until fully repaid through payroll deductions Retirement investments remain untouched and continue compounding uninterrupted in financial markets 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Choose a 401(k) loan if your job is stable, you need $50,000 or less, you want to avoid lender closing costs, appraisals, and credit checks, and you have a clear plan to repay the balance within five years. Choose a HELOC if you have substantial home equity, want to leave your retirement savings fully invested to maximize compound growth, require revolving access to larger credit lines, and plan to use the money for home improvements where interest may qualify for a tax deduction. This advice is not for workers navigating unstable corporate restructurings or volatile employment situations, where an unexpected layoff would instantly turn an unpaid 401(k) loan into a punishing taxable distribution with a 10% penalty. Our recommendation would change if your employer's plan document prohibits participant loans entirely, or if local property values drop so significantly that you cannot satisfy standard bank equity thresholds to open a credit line. Before making a final choice on a 401k loan vs HELOC, check your employer's summary plan description with your plan administrator and calculate the exact distribution tax consequences on our 401(k) Early Withdrawal Calculator . What Decides Between a 401(k) Loan and a HELOC Choosing between a 401(k) loan and a HELOC depends on whether you have sufficient home equity and whether your employment is stable enough to avoid accelerated repayment rules. If you borrow from your workplace retirement account, the primary operational hazard centers on your job status. When an employee leaves or loses their position with an outstanding loan balance, federal tax guidelines accelerate the repayment timeline. Failing to settle that balance by the deadline converts the outstanding debt into a taxable withdrawal, generating an unexpected tax liability. Conversely, a home equity line of credit introduces physical asset risk, because defaulting on a secured bank line allows the lender to initiate foreclosure on your residence. The decision also hinges on qualification barriers and upfront costs. Opening a HELOC requires undergoing a thorough underwriting evaluation, including a review of your credit report, income verification, and a professional property appraisal to establish your loan-to-value (LTV) ratio. A 401(k) loan bypasses credit bureaus entirely because you are borrowing your own accumulated capital under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 72(p). If you have a damaged credit history or require rapid liquidity without paying loan origination fees, a retirement loan offers a much faster administrative path. To see how much your balance lets you borrow and what the payment would be, use our 401(k) loan calculator . For readers coordinating broader household savings strategies, our Retirement Hub provides detailed frameworks on structuring assets across multiple accounts. Comparing a 401k Loan vs HELOC for Home Improvement A HELOC is generally the superior choice for home improvement projects because it offers revolving access to cash and potential tax deductibility that a 401(k) loan cannot match. Major home renovations rarely incur all expenses at once, often rolling out in phases over several months. A HELOC accommodates this workflow through an initial draw period that typically spans up to 10 years, allowing you to pull funds only when contractor invoices arrive while paying interest exclusively on the active balance. According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) , variable interest rates on home equity lines in 2026 run roughly 8.5% to 9.5%. You can model these variable payment structures using our HELOC calculator guide before committing your residential equity. The federal tax code also provides a meaningful structural advantage for home renovations financed through real estate equity. Under Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Publication 936 , interest paid on a home equity line of credit is federally tax-deductible if the borrowed proceeds are used to buy, build, or substantially improve the residence securing the credit line. In contrast, interest on a 401(k) loan is never tax-deductible under any circumstance, because you are remitting interest payments back to yourself. While repaying interest to your own account provides personal satisfaction, pulling capital out of equity keeps your retirement portfolio fully invested while opening up a potential tax deduction if you itemize. The Job Separation Risk of Retirement Borrowing Leaving an employer with an active 401(k) loan accelerates your repayment schedule and can trigger immediate tax liabilities if you cannot pay off the balance. Federal rules under IRC Section 72(p) govern how workplace retirement plans administer participant borrowing, as outlined by the Internal Revenue Service . Under standard plan guidelines, an active employee repays their loan over a maximum five-year term through automatic payroll deductions. However, if you voluntarily resign, experience a corporate layoff, or face termination, those automated payroll deductions cease immediately. Current federal tax law gives separated workers until the due date of their federal tax return for that tax year, including extensions, to repay the outstanding balance in full. If you lack the liquid capital to pay off that accelerated balance by the tax deadline, the unpaid loan amount is officially classified as a deemed distribution. The entire remaining principal is added directly to your gross taxable income for that calendar year, subjecting you to ordinary state and federal income tax brackets. Furthermore, if you are under age 59½, the IRS imposes a mandatory 10% early-withdrawal penalty on that taxable sum. You can calculate the exact cash cost of an unintended distribution with our 401(k) Early Withdrawal Calculator before tapping your vested workplace balance. Collateral Requirements and Foreclosure Exposure with Home Equity Borrowing against residential equity through a HELOC avoids putting your retirement funds at risk but exposes your home to foreclosure if you fall behind on payments. Unlike a 401(k) loan where you borrow from your personal assets, a HELOC is a third-party commercial debt instrument secured by a legal lien against your property deed. If an unforeseen financial emergency or prolonged income disruption prevents you from making the required monthly interest or principal payments, the lending institution holds the legal right to foreclose on the property to recover its capital. This foreclosure exposure represents a fundamental hazard that retirement loans do not share, where default triggers tax consequences rather than the loss of your home. Securing a home equity line also requires satisfying rigorous bank underwriting standards that workplace retirement plans do not mandate. Lenders review your credit score across major reporting agencies, evaluate your overall debt-to-income ratio, and demand an appraisal to confirm sufficient equity above existing mortgage balances. If your credit score is below prime thresholds or your local housing market has experienced price drops, lenders can reject your application or charge high variable margins. If you want to evaluate home equity against non-collateral alternatives, review our comparison of a HELOC vs Personal Loan to weigh unsecured options. Evaluating a 401k Loan vs HELOC for Down Payment Needs Using a 401(k) loan for a home down payment provides fast liquidity without adding a lien on your existing property, but statutory borrowing limits restrict its utility for larger purchases. Federal regulations cap 401(k) borrowing at the lesser of 50% of your vested balance or $50,000. While plan administrators frequently allow extended repayment schedules beyond five years when the loan is explicitly used to acquire a primary residence, a $50,000 cap may fall short of what buyers require in competitive real estate markets. A HELOC can provide substantially larger borrowing amounts if your current home has accrued meaningful equity, limited only by your lender's allowable LTV ratio. Retirement borrowing also incurs an unavoidable opportunity cost that home equity borrowing avoids. Every dollar removed from your retirement account stops generating investment earnings, compounding interest, and corporate dividend payouts until you repay the funds. Even though your repayment interest goes back into your account, that fixed rate rarely matches the multi-year compound performance of a diversified equity market index. Borrowing $50,000 right before an extended market expansion can permanently depress your future retirement wealth, costing far more in missed compounding than the fees saved by skipping a bank loan. Frequently asked questions What are the drawbacks of taking out a 401(k) loan? The primary drawback of a 401(k) loan is the risk of accelerated repayment if you separate from your employer, which converts unpaid debt into a taxable distribution with potential penalties. Additionally, money borrowed stops earning compound market returns, and loans are federally capped at the lesser of 50% of your vested balance or $50,000. Is a 401(k) loan or a HELOC better for a down payment? A HELOC is often better if you need more than $50,000 and own a primary home with extensive equity, while a 401(k) loan works well for smaller down payments if you have no current home to borrow against. A 401(k) loan also allows extended repayment terms beyond five years when purchasing a primary home, though plan rules dictate the exact duration. What happens to a 401(k) loan if I lose my job? If you leave or lose your job with an outstanding 401(k) loan balance, your automatic payroll deductions stop immediately. Under federal tax law, you generally have until the due date of your federal tax return for that year, including extensions, to repay the balance; any unpaid funds become a taxable distribution subject to income tax and a 10% penalty if you are under age 59½. Is 401(k) loan interest tax-deductible like HELOC interest can be? No, 401(k) loan interest is never tax-deductible because you are paying the interest directly back into your own personal retirement account. HELOC interest, by comparison, may be tax-deductible if you itemize deductions and use the borrowed proceeds specifically to buy, build, or substantially improve the property securing the line of credit. Do I need good credit for a 401(k) loan? No, you do not need good credit to qualify for a 401(k) loan because there is no credit check, credit bureau reporting, or third-party underwriting involved. You are borrowing against your own vested balance under plan guidelines, unlike a HELOC which requires a solid credit score, income verification, and an appraisal. How the SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) funding rules differ The core split in the SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) debate is who puts money in. A SEP-IRA is funded by the business only. You can contribute up to 25% of your compensation, capped at $70,000 in 2025. A Solo 401(k) works in two layers. First, you make an employee salary deferral of up to $23,500 in 2025. Second, the business adds a profit-sharing contribution. Together they can reach the same $70,000 cap. That second layer is why the accounts behave so differently at lower incomes. See our 401(k) vs Roth IRA guide for how deferrals fit a wider plan. Why a Solo 401(k) lets you save more at modest income At a modest income, a Solo 401(k) usually lets you contribute more than a SEP-IRA. This is the non-obvious tradeoff many people miss. Here is a simple decision rule. Suppose you earn $60,000 in net self-employment income. A SEP-IRA caps you near 25% of pay, roughly $15,000. A Solo 401(k) lets you defer $23,500 as the employee first, then add the employer share on top. So the same person can save far more in the Solo 401(k). The SEP-IRA only catches up at high incomes, where both plans hit the $70,000 ceiling. Model your gap with our retirement savings calculator . Roth, loans, and paperwork: the features that break the tie A Solo 401(k) offers Roth contributions and loans, while a SEP-IRA offers neither. If you want tax-free growth through Roth dollars, the Solo 401(k) is the only choice here. A Solo 401(k) can also let you borrow from the plan if the document permits it. A SEP-IRA never allows a loan. To see a solo 401(k) loan's limit and payment, use our solo 401(k) loan calculator . The cost is more admin. Once your Solo 401(k) assets pass $250,000, you must file Form 5500-EZ each year. A SEP-IRA has no such annual filing, which keeps it simple. The employee rule is the key limit. A Solo 401(k) is for owner-only businesses, meaning you and a spouse with no other full-time staff. If you hire a full-time employee, the Solo 401(k) no longer fits. A SEP-IRA still works with employees. But you must contribute the same percentage of pay for every eligible worker, which can get expensive. If you'd rather offer a full workplace plan, compare setups in our best small-business 401(k) providers roundup. Compare account types in our brokerage vs IRA guide. How to choose between a SEP-IRA and a Solo 401(k) To choose in the SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) decision, start with two questions: do you have employees, and how much do you want to save? If you are owner-only and want to maximize savings, add Roth money, or borrow, choose the Solo 401(k). If you are owner-only but want zero paperwork and earn enough to hit the 25% cap anyway, the SEP-IRA is a clean fit. Check your overall picture with our net worth tracker . A Solo 401(k) also allows a $23,500 employee deferral within that cap, plus a catch-up that raises the ceiling to $77,500 for those age 50 or older. A SEP-IRA is limited to 25% of compensation up to the $70,000 cap. Which plan is simpler to set up and run? A SEP-IRA is simpler to set up and run. It opens in minutes and has no annual IRS filing. Yes, you can switch from a SEP-IRA to a Solo 401(k) if you are owner-only. Many self-employed savers move to a Solo 401(k) to add Roth dollars or to contribute more at modest income. mainEntity.name: Can I contribute more to a SEP-IRA or a Solo 401(k)?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can usually contribute more to a Solo 401(k), especially at modest income. Both cap at $70,000 in 2025, but the Solo 401(k) adds a $23,500 employee deferral on top of the employer share. That flat deferral lets you save more than a SEP-IRA's 25% limit until your income is high enough to max both.

mainEntity.name: Does a SEP-IRA allow Roth contributions?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, a SEP-IRA does not allow Roth contributions. Only a Solo 401(k) lets you make Roth deferrals for tax-free growth. If Roth savings matter to you, the Solo 401(k) is the plan that offers them.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a Solo 401(k) if I have employees?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, you cannot use a Solo 401(k) if you have non-spouse full-time employees. A Solo 401(k) is for owner-only businesses, including a spouse who works in the business. If you have other full-time staff, use a SEP-IRA instead, and you must fund the same percentage for each eligible worker.

mainEntity.name: What are the 2025 SEP-IRA and Solo 401(k) limits?

acceptedAnswer.text: For 2025, both plans cap total contributions at $70,000. A Solo 401(k) also allows a $23,500 employee deferral within that cap, plus a catch-up that raises the ceiling to $77,500 for those age 50 or older. A SEP-IRA is limited to 25% of compensation up to the $70,000 cap.

mainEntity.name: Which plan is simpler to set up and run?

acceptedAnswer.text: A SEP-IRA is simpler to set up and run. It opens in minutes and has no annual IRS filing. A Solo 401(k) needs more paperwork and requires Form 5500-EZ once plan assets exceed $250,000, though it offers Roth and loan features a SEP-IRA lacks.

mainEntity.name: Can I switch from a SEP-IRA to a Solo 401(k)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, you can switch from a SEP-IRA to a Solo 401(k) if you are owner-only. Many self-employed savers move to a Solo 401(k) to add Roth dollars or to contribute more at modest income. Ask your provider about rolling SEP-IRA balances and check the timing rules for the year of the switch.

By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated June 25, 2026 A bridge loan is a short-term loan (usually 6 to 12 months) secured by the equity in your current home. It can fund the down payment on a new home before your old one sells and sometimes pays off your existing mortgage at the same closing. A home equity line of credit (HELOC) uses that same equity through a revolving credit line. It typically costs less, but takes longer to open and cannot retire your existing mortgage the way a bridge loan can. Choose a bridge loan if your closing date is only weeks away and speed matters more than price. Choose a HELOC if you have several weeks of lead time and want the lower-cost option. Bridge Loan vs HELOC: Side-by-Side Bridge Loan HELOC Speed to close 1 to 3 weeks, built for a tight purchase deadline 2 to 6 weeks, requires appraisal and underwriting Typical rate Prime rate plus 1 to 3 percentage points Prime rate plus 0 to 2 percentage points Term 6 to 12 months, short and self-liquidating 10-year draw period, then a 10 to 20-year repayment period Fees and closing costs Origination and closing fees typically 1.5% to 3% of the loan amount Often $0 to $500; some lenders cover the appraisal Secured by Equity in your current home, sometimes cross-collateralized with the new one Equity in your current home only What it can cover Down payment on the new home and payoff of the current mortgage in one loan Down payment or closing costs; it does not pay off your existing mortgage balance Payment structure Often interest-only until the old home sells Interest-only during the draw period, then principal plus interest Best use case A firm purchase deadline with an unsold current home Equity access with a few weeks of lead time and no hard purchase deadline 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Choose a bridge loan when you have a signed purchase contract on the new home and your current one has not sold yet. Its speed, and the option to fold your existing mortgage payoff into one loan, justify the higher rate and the origination fee. Choose a HELOC when you have at least three to four weeks before you need the funds. Your current mortgage balance also has to leave enough room under an 80% combined loan-to-value limit. A HELOC will not retire your existing mortgage, so a buyer carrying a large balance on the departing home usually needs the bridge loan's single-loan structure instead. If your current home is already under contract with a firm closing date, the sale-timing risk behind the bridge loan's extra cost disappears. The HELOC becomes the cheaper choice at that point. Run your own numbers through the home affordability calculator before you apply for either one. How a Bridge Loan Works for a Home Purchase A bridge loan is a short-term loan secured by the equity in your current home, structured to close fast enough to meet a new purchase deadline. Terms typically run 6 to 12 months, long enough to sell the old home without forcing a rushed sale. Rates typically run at the prime rate plus 1 to 3 percentage points, and many bridge loans are interest-only, so the monthly payment stays lower while you carry two properties at once. Origination and closing fees typically run 1.5% to 3% of the loan amount, on top of the rate. To price your own sale timeline, use our bridge loan calculator . The structural advantage over a HELOC is what the loan can cover. A bridge loan can be sized to pay off your current mortgage in full and still leave enough for the down payment on the new home, all in one closing. That single-loan structure is why a bridge lender can often move faster than a standard HELOC underwriter. The lender prices the sale of your current home into the deal from day one, rather than treating it as a side fact. How a HELOC Works for This Same Scenario A HELOC is a revolving line of credit against your home's equity, and buyers in this situation use it to fund the down payment on a new home before their current one sells. You draw only what you need, and interest accrues only on the amount you have drawn, not the full approved line. Rates typically run at the prime rate plus 0 to 2 percentage points, lower than a bridge loan because the lender is not pricing in the same closing-timeline risk. Closing costs are usually much lighter too. Many lenders charge $0 to $500, and some absorb the appraisal fee entirely. The tradeoff is speed. Opening a HELOC typically takes 2 to 6 weeks, since the lender still orders an appraisal and underwrites the line the way it would any other loan. Most lenders also want a credit score of 680 or higher and a combined loan-to-value under 80% to 85% before approving it. A HELOC has a hard limit a bridge loan does not share: it cannot pay off your existing mortgage. According to the CFPB , the 80% to 85% combined loan-to-value ceiling is standard across most HELOC lenders. That ceiling is why a homeowner with a large existing mortgage balance often finds the available HELOC amount too small to cover both a down payment and a mortgage payoff at the same time. The Cost Comparison Over a Realistic 6- to 12-Month Hold The cost gap between a bridge loan and a HELOC over a realistic 6- to 12-month hold comes mostly from the origination fee, not the rate difference. Take a homeowner borrowing $70,000 for a down payment, with a bridge loan priced at prime plus 2 points and a HELOC priced at prime plus 1 point. Using an illustrative prime rate of 7.5%, the bridge loan carries a 9.5% rate and the HELOC carries an 8.5% rate. Actual rates move with the Federal Reserve's benchmark and vary by lender. Over 6 months, interest-only payments on the bridge loan total about $3,325. Add a 2% origination fee of $1,400, and the bridge loan costs roughly $4,725 for the half-year hold. The HELOC's interest over the same 6 months runs about $2,975, and with a typical $300 closing cost, its total lands near $3,275. The bridge loan costs about $1,450 more in this example. Stretch the hold to 12 months, the outer edge of a typical bridge loan term, and the shape of the gap changes. The bridge loan's interest doubles to about $6,650, but the origination fee stays fixed at $1,400, for a total near $8,050. The HELOC's interest also doubles, to about $5,950, plus the same $300 closing cost, for a total near $6,250. The dollar gap widens to about $1,800, even as the origination fee's share of the total cost shrinks. A 1-percentage-point rate spread sounds small, but it compounds every month you carry the balance, which is what a quick glance at the two rates alone misses. These figures are illustrative. Your own rate, loan amount, and lender fees will differ, so run your actual numbers through the closing cost calculator before comparing offers. To change the hold period, calculate your own bridge loan cost . A calculator for short-term interest-only loans prices a different short-term loan from your own quote. When to Use Each A bridge loan and a HELOC usually come down to timeline more than budget. The deciding factor is how many weeks you have before you need the money. A bridge loan fits when you have a signed contract on the new home and closing is fewer than three weeks away. It also fits when your current mortgage balance is large enough that a HELOC's borrowing limit would not cover both the down payment and the mortgage payoff. A HELOC fits when you have four or more weeks before you need funds and your current home carries a modest mortgage balance relative to its value. It also fits a homeowner who wants to open a credit line early, before listing the house, and draw from it only once a purchase is close to closing. A bridge loan is not the right tool for a homeowner who has not yet listed their current home and has no firm sale timeline. Carrying two mortgage-sized payments for an open-ended stretch turns the bridge loan's short term into a real risk instead of a bridge. In that situation, a HELOC opened well ahead of the purchase, or simply waiting to list the current home first, usually costs less and carries less risk. If your current home sale is already under contract with a scheduled closing, both options carry less risk, and the HELOC's lower cost usually wins unless your remaining mortgage balance is too large for the line to cover. Compare both against your full purchase budget with the home affordability calculator , and see how a HELOC compares to a home equity loan if you decide you don't need the speed a bridge loan buys. Frequently asked questions Can I use a HELOC as a bridge loan? Yes, and many homeowners do exactly this. You open the HELOC while you still own your current home, draw the funds for the new home's down payment when you need them, and repay the line once your current home sells. The tradeoff is that a HELOC will not pay off your existing mortgage, so this approach works best when your remaining mortgage balance is small enough that a standard down payment closes the gap without a true bridge loan's higher borrowing power. What happens if my home doesn't sell in time on a bridge loan? Most bridge lenders offer a short extension, often for an added fee, but you're still on the hook for the full loan plus interest until the home sells. Some lenders charge a penalty rate or convert the loan's terms after the original term expires. If your home still hasn't sold after an extension, you may need to refinance the bridge loan into a longer-term loan or lower your asking price to force a faster sale. Is a bridge loan riskier than a HELOC? Yes, mainly because you're carrying two mortgage-sized obligations at once against a shorter, harder deadline. A HELOC's draw-as-needed structure and its longer repayment window spread that risk out over more time. A bridge loan's compressed term means a slow home sale turns into financial pressure faster than it would with a HELOC. Do I need to qualify for both mortgages at once? Usually yes, for either option. Lenders typically count your current mortgage payment, your new mortgage payment, and the bridge loan or HELOC payment in your debt-to-income ratio, unless your current home is already under a signed sale contract. Some bridge lenders exclude the departing home's mortgage from that calculation once the sale contract is firm, which is one reason a bridge loan can be easier to qualify for than it first appears. Which is cheaper, a bridge loan or a HELOC? A HELOC is almost always cheaper on paper, with a lower rate and lower closing costs. But cheaper only matters if it closes in time. If a HELOC's 2- to 6-week timeline doesn't fit your purchase deadline, the bridge loan's higher cost buys the speed a HELOC cannot. Can I open a HELOC before I list my home for sale? Yes, and doing so early is often the better move. Opening the HELOC while you still show strong income and an on-time mortgage payment history works in your favor during underwriting. Waiting until after you list the home, or after an offer is pending, can make qualifying harder if a lender treats the pending sale as added uncertainty. Being a landlord is one option, but short-term rentals, house flipping, REITs, and real estate crowdfunding also let you invest in property, each with very different levels of cash, time, and risk. This guide compares all five, including the tax rules and liquidity tradeoffs that most overviews skip, so you can choose the option that actually fits your money and schedule. Tools for this journey Rental cash flow → Cap rate → Airbnb income → Net worth → Option 1: Being a landlord Being a landlord means buying a property and renting it out for monthly income, the most hands-on option on this list. You collect rent, pay the mortgage, taxes, and insurance, and keep what's left as cash flow, while tenants slowly pay down your loan and build your equity. The IRS also lets you depreciate the building over 27.5 years, which can shelter real rental income from tax on paper. The tradeoff is real, ongoing work: tenant screening, repairs, vacancies, and the occasional late-night maintenance call, unless you pay a property manager 8% to 12% of rent to handle it. Landlording rewards people who run the numbers before they buy, not just people who like the idea of owning property. ModernWallet already covers this option in depth. Run your own numbers with our rental cash flow calculator and cap rate calculator before you make an offer — a property with negative cash flow is a bet on appreciation, not an investment that pays you today. Option 2: Running a short-term rental A short-term rental is a home or spare room you rent out by the night instead of by the year, most often through Airbnb or a similar booking platform. It can earn more per night than a long-term lease in tourist or event-driven markets, but it also adds turnover cleaning, guest messaging, and dynamic pricing that a long-term rental never requires. Most overviews skip the two traps that catch new hosts. First, many cities and HOAs now require a short-term rental permit, cap the nights you can rent per year, or ban them outright in certain zones — check your local ordinance before you list a property, not after. Second, the tax treatment can shift: rental income is usually reported on Schedule E and isn't subject to self-employment tax, but a short-term rental that provides hotel-like services (daily cleaning, breakfast, concierge) can be treated as a trade or business, taxed on Schedule C and hit with self-employment tax on top of income tax. Model the income side with our Airbnb income calculator , then confirm the local rules and likely tax treatment before you commit a property to short-term use. Option 3: Flipping houses Flipping a house means buying a property below market value, renovating it, and reselling it quickly for a profit, usually within months rather than years. Experienced flippers often use the 70% rule as a first screen: pay no more than 70% of a property's after-repair value, minus your estimated repair costs, to leave margin for the unexpected. Financing a flip adds its own cost, which our hard money loan calculator prices from your lender's terms. The tax trap is the part most guides skip. Sell within a year and the profit is taxed as a short-term capital gain at your ordinary income tax rate, not the lower long-term rate — IRS Topic No. 409 covers the distinction. Flip houses often enough and the IRS may classify you as a real estate dealer rather than an investor, which adds self-employment tax on top of that and blocks a 1031 like-kind exchange, a tool that only applies to investment property, not inventory you're actively selling. Flipping can pay well, but it's the most active, most tax-exposed option on this list — closer to running a small business than making a passive investment. Option 4: REITs (real estate investment trusts) A REIT, or real estate investment trust, is a company that owns income-producing property and must pay out most of its profit as dividends, so you get real estate exposure just by buying a share the same way you'd buy a stock. The SEC explains that publicly traded REITs trade on major exchanges and can be bought or sold on any trading day, while non-traded REITs are illiquid and can restrict how much you're allowed to redeem in a given period. The tax tradeoff is the piece most beginners miss. Because a REIT avoids corporate income tax by distributing at least 90% of its taxable income, most REIT dividends are taxed to you as ordinary income instead of at the lower qualified-dividend rate — though the IRS does let individuals deduct up to 20% of that ordinary REIT dividend income, which softens the gap for many investors. A REIT gives you real estate exposure with stock-market liquidity and zero landlord duties, the most passive option on this list — but you give up the direct control, leverage, and depreciation benefits that come with owning property outright. Option 5: Real estate crowdfunding Real estate crowdfunding lets you invest smaller amounts alongside other investors in a specific property or fund through an online platform, instead of buying a whole property yourself. Not every platform is open to every investor, and that distinction matters more than the marketing suggests. Platforms raising money through Regulation Crowdfunding (Reg CF) must open the offering to non-accredited investors too, though the SEC caps how much a non-accredited investor can put in over a 12-month period based on their income and net worth. Platforms raising money under Regulation D are usually restricted to accredited investors — generally, individual income over $200,000 (or $300,000 with a spouse) in each of the last two years, or a net worth over $1 million excluding your primary residence. Check which exemption a platform is using before you fund an account, since it determines both who can invest and how much disclosure you're entitled to see. Crowdfunding sits between a REIT and a direct rental purchase: less liquid than a REIT, but far less work than owning and managing a property yourself. The bottom line: how the 5 options compare The five real estate investment options trade off liquidity, active work, and tax complexity in a fairly predictable pattern. Being a landlord and flipping houses demand the most hands-on time and the most tax complexity, but they also offer the most control and, for landlording, the steadiest long-run cash flow. A short-term rental sits in between: less commitment than a long-term rental, but real day-to-day management and a local-ordinance risk unique to this option. REITs and real estate crowdfunding sit at the more passive end. A REIT is the most liquid of the five — you can sell in seconds during market hours — while crowdfunding is less liquid but often lets you target a specific property or strategy a broad REIT fund wouldn't. There's no single best answer. Want real estate exposure with no landlord duties and full liquidity? A REIT is the simplest starting point. Have more time than capital and want control over one property? Landlording or a short-term rental fits better. Want to test the waters with a small amount first? Crowdfunding is the middle ground. Whichever you choose, check your own net worth first, since your real estate allocation should scale with what you can actually afford to tie up or lose. Frequently asked questions What's the easiest real estate investment for beginners? For most beginners, a publicly traded REIT is the easiest option because it requires no property management, trades like a stock, and can be bought with any amount of money. Being a landlord or flipping houses both require far more capital, time, and tax planning to do well. Are REITs a good investment? REITs can be a good investment for hands-off real estate exposure, since the SEC requires them to distribute at least 90% of taxable income as dividends. Most of that income is taxed as ordinary income rather than at lower qualified-dividend rates, though a deduction on ordinary REIT dividends softens that gap for many investors. How much money do I need to start real estate crowdfunding? It depends on the platform and which SEC exemption it uses. Platforms using Regulation Crowdfunding are open to non-accredited investors with online investment limits based on income and net worth, while platforms restricted to accredited investors require you to meet the SEC's income or net worth thresholds first. Is house flipping profit taxed as ordinary income? Yes, if you hold the property for a year or less, the profit is taxed as a short-term capital gain at your ordinary income tax rate. Flip houses often enough and the IRS may also classify you as a dealer, adding self-employment tax on top and blocking access to a 1031 exchange. Do I need a permit to run a short-term rental? Often yes. Many cities and homeowner associations require a permit, cap the nights you can rent per year, or restrict short-term rentals to certain zones entirely. Check your local ordinance before you list a property, since rules vary widely even between neighboring cities. Which real estate investment option has the best returns? There's no single option with the best returns for everyone; it depends on the leverage, work, and risk you're willing to take on. Flipping and landlording can post the highest returns because of leverage and active management, but REITs and crowdfunding trade some upside for far less time, work, and concentration risk. Cash-on-cash return is calculated by dividing annual pre-tax cash flow by total cash invested. Enter your numbers in the calculator above to see your percentage in seconds. It answers one question: How hard is my invested cash working this year? $290 monthly cash flow 7.23% cap rate 4.98% cash-on-cash Share Interactive — edit any field How it's calculated The cash on cash return calculator divides your annual pre-tax cash flow by the total cash you invested. Cash flow is your rental income minus operating expenses and your mortgage payment. Total cash invested is your down payment plus closing costs, not the full purchase price. Here is a non-obvious point. Cash-on-cash measures cash flow only. It ignores appreciation, loan paydown, and tax benefits, so it understates your total return. It is also a year-one snapshot. As rents rise over time, your cash-on-cash return usually climbs too. For the full picture, pair it with our ROI calculator . A worked example Consider a $250,000 rental bought with 25% down and 3% closing costs. Your total cash invested is $70,000. The loan is $187,500 at 6.75% over 30 years, so monthly principal and interest is $1,216. Rent is $2,350 per month, or $28,200 a year. After 5% vacancy, effective gross income is $26,790. Operating expenses total $8,712, leaving net operating income of $18,078. Subtract the mortgage payments and annual cash flow is $3,485, or about $290 a month. Divide $3,485 by $70,000 and the cash-on-cash return is 4.98%. For comparison, the cap rate is 7.23% and the DSCR is 1.24. Common mistakes to avoid Using the full purchase price as cash invested. Use only your down payment plus closing costs, not the financed amount. If the loan is short-term and interest-only, price its points and interest first with our short-term loan cost calculator . Forgetting vacancy. Always reduce gross rent for expected empty months before you calculate cash flow. Leaving out maintenance and management. These ongoing costs shrink cash flow and lower your true return. Confusing cash-on-cash with cap rate. Cap rate ignores your mortgage; cash-on-cash includes it. Treating it as total return. Cash-on-cash skips appreciation, loan paydown, and tax perks, so it understates lifetime gains. Frequently asked questions What is a cash on cash return calculator? A cash on cash return calculator divides your annual pre-tax cash flow by the total cash you invested in a property. It returns a percentage that shows the yield on your actual money. The calculator above does this instantly once you enter rent, expenses, and your down payment. See our cash flow calculator to build the cash flow figure. What is a good cash-on-cash return? Many investors target a cash-on-cash return of 8% to 12%, though good depends on your market and goals. In the example above, a 4.98% return is on the lower side. Compare it against other deals and safer options like bonds before you buy. How is cash-on-cash return different from cap rate? Cash-on-cash return includes your mortgage payments, while cap rate ignores financing entirely. Cap rate divides net operating income by property value. Cash-on-cash divides cash flow by the cash you invested. In the example, the cap rate is 7.23% and cash-on-cash is 4.98%. Our cap rate calculator handles that metric. Does cash-on-cash return include appreciation? No. Cash-on-cash return measures cash flow only. It ignores appreciation, loan paydown, and tax benefits, so it understates your total return.
